Evaluating Escalation Signals for LLM Routing:
Targets, Controls, and Five Ways to Fool Yourself

Ramin Pishehvar Affiliation: Cisco Systems, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA
{rpishehv, amoranid, mahviswa}@cisco.com    Andrea Morandi Affiliation: Cisco Systems, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA
{rpishehv, amoranid, mahviswa}@cisco.com Affiliation: Cisco Systems, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA
{rpishehv, amoranid, mahviswa}@cisco.com    Mahesh Viswanathan Affiliation: Cisco Systems, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA
{rpishehv, amoranid, mahviswa}@cisco.com
Abstract

Deciding when to escalate a query from a small language model to a larger one requires a cheap signal that can predict, before the large model is ever called, whether escalating would actually help. Semantic entropy, originally developed to detect hallucinations, is a natural candidate: it measures how much a model’s own sampled answers disagree in meaning, and high disagreement often signals an unreliable answer. We test it as an escalation signal across three benchmarks and two model families. On GSM8K, with a small/large model pair about twelve times apart in size, semantic entropy reliably distinguishes the small model’s mistakes (AUROC 0.871) and improves routed accuracy over random escalation by up to nine points at matched cost. An earlier, similarly strong-looking result on a synthetic arithmetic benchmark turned out to be misleading: a simple rule based only on how hard a question looks on the page, with no model involved at all, matched semantic entropy’s performance almost exactly.

This paper’s main contribution is a set of checks that catch this kind of misleading result before it is reported as real. We show that scoring a cheap, question-only difficulty estimate alongside any signal reveals whether that signal is adding real information or just tracking how hard a question looks; that two reasonable-seeming definitions of "the escalation worked" can produce very different results on the same data; that a benchmark can leave almost no room for any signal to beat simply always using the large model, however good that signal is; and that the true cost of gathering a live signal, querying the small model many times per question, can make routing more expensive than just calling the large model directly. For a cheaper alternative that reuses cached past outcomes instead of live sampling, we show how to predict, before running an experiment, whether that shortcut will work on a new dataset, confirmed by correctly forecasting a collapse from a strong-looking result (AUROC 0.908) to a chance-level one (0.518) ahead of time. We offer these as a general checklist for evaluating escalation signals, not as a case for this one.

1 Introduction

Serving every query with the largest available language model is wasteful: many queries are easy enough for a small model (SLM) to answer correctly, and only a minority need the extra capacity of a large model (LLM). A router that can cheaply predict, before querying the large model, whether a given query needs it would let a system pay the large model’s cost only when it is worth paying.

Semantic entropy [1] is a natural candidate signal. Originally proposed for hallucination detection, it estimates a model’s uncertainty about the meaning of its own answer: draw kk stochastic samples for a query, cluster them by bidirectional NLI entailment (two samples belong to the same cluster iff each entails the other), and compute the Shannon entropy of the resulting cluster-probability distribution. High semantic entropy indicates that the model’s samples disagree on meaning, not just wording – a stronger hallucination signal than lexical diversity or output confidence alone. Our implementation clusters a terse extracted answer rather than the raw generation (Section 5) and takes plain cluster frequency rather than weighting by the model’s own sequence probabilities as in [1]; this is closer to the discrete, frequency-weighted self-consistency of [2] than to full semantic entropy, and we use the term throughout to mean this specific, cheaper variant.

This paper asks: can semantic entropy, computed from the small model’s own samples, predict whether escalating a query to a large model would improve the answer? We build a full pipeline to test this, run it across three benchmarks and two model families, and report both positive and negative results, several real implementation bugs encountered along the way, and a conceptual clarification of what semantic entropy can and cannot be expected to predict.

2 Related Work

Cascades and routing.

Cascading – serving most queries with a cheap model and escalating hard ones – was popularized by FrugalGPT [8], which learns confidence thresholds over a portfolio of commercial APIs and reports large cost reductions at matched quality. AutoMix [10] wraps few-shot self-verification in a POMDP-based router requiring only API access. A parallel line performs pre-generation routing, selecting one model before any inference: RouteLLM [9] and Hybrid LLM [13] learn such a router from preference data, the latter adding an explicit quality-cost objective. The distinction matters for our cost analysis: a pre-generation router never pays the small model, whereas a cascade pays it on every query – and, in our setting, pays it kk times (Section 3.5).

Uncertainty signals for deferral.

Token-level confidence is the established deferral signal for generative cascades, tracing back to the classical error-reject tradeoff [19]; Gupta et al. [7] formalize the Chow-style variants (summed and length-normalized log-probability, and quantiles thereof) that our avg_neg_logprob instantiates. Semantic uncertainty [4] and its refinement into semantic entropy [1] were introduced for hallucination detection rather than routing.

Agreement-based deferral.

The closest prior work to ours is Soiffer et al. [5], who use semantic agreement among an ensemble of distinct small models as a training-free deferral signal, reporting quality matching a 70B target at 40% of its compute budget. Related, Kolawole et al. [6] use ensemble agreement for cascade deferral and Yue et al. [12] use answer consistency for numerical reasoning. Our setting differs in construction – kk stochastic samples from a single model, clustered by bidirectional NLI entailment with entropy over the cluster distribution, following [1] – but the underlying intuition, that meaning-level disagreement indicates unreliability, is shared. We regard the effectiveness of this family as established by that work rather than as our contribution.

What this paper adds.

Several of our findings corroborate results reached independently, which we take as evidence that they are properties of the problem rather than of our implementation. Soiffer et al. report that agreement-based deferral degrades on short-answer closed-book QA, where answers are brief and baseline accuracy is low, and that token-level confidence overtakes it there. We observe a related difficulty on PopQA, for a different reason: escalation itself is the wrong intervention there, since both models lack the needed parametric knowledge rather than disagreeing on it (Section 6.4) – we did not reach an entropy-vs-confidence comparison on PopQA, having abandoned signal evaluation there once the headroom failure was established. On synthetic arithmetic we find the mirror image of Soiffer et al.’s result instead: token confidence is the signal that inverts, falling below chance across four independent measurements (Section 6.5). The concern motivating our per-generation cost accounting – that kk-sample estimation changes the serving cost model – is precisely why at least one recent cascade system declines to use semantic entropy at all.

Our contribution is therefore not the signal but the evaluation methodology. To our knowledge, no prior cascade study reports a difficulty baseline: the deferral literature compares against token-level confidence, random deferral, and learned routers, but not against what the question text alone already reveals. On our synthetic benchmark that baseline is free and matches semantic entropy exactly, nullifying a result we had initially accepted (Section 6.5); on GSM8K entropy beats it by a wide margin (Section 6.1), and the two cases are indistinguishable without the control. Nor, to our knowledge, does prior work report an oracle-headroom precondition, the difficulty-calibrated variant needed to evaluate retrieval-based routers fairly, or the observation that on lexically regular benchmarks an embedding space can encode difficulty so completely (ρ=0.98\rho=0.98) that nearest-neighbor retrieval is difficulty lookup – a diagnostic that correctly forecast the collapse of an apparent retrieval result on a benchmark not yet run (Section 7). Selective prediction [11] supplies the abstention framework these controls operate within.

3 Method

3.1 Semantic entropy

Given a query qq and kk stochastic samples y1,…,yky_{1},\ldots,y_{k} drawn from a model at temperature >0>0, we cluster the samples via bidirectional entailment, following the semantic-uncertainty construction of [4] and its refinement into semantic entropy by [1], using an NLI model (microsoft/deberta-large-mnli [17]): yiy_{i} and yjy_{j} are placed in the same cluster iff P⁡(entail∣yi,yj)>τP(\text{entail}\mid y_{i},y_{j})>\tau and P⁡(entail∣yj,yi)>τP(\text{entail}\mid y_{j},y_{i})>\tau, for threshold τ=0.5\tau=0.5. Writing C1,…,CmC_{1},\ldots,C_{m} for the resulting clusters and p⁡(Cc)=|Cc|/kp(C_{c})=|C_{c}|/k for the empirical cluster probability, semantic entropy is

H=−∑c=1mp(Cc)logp(Cc),H=-\sum_{c=1}^{m}p(C_{c})\log p(C_{c}), (1)

and the normalized form used throughout this work is Hnorm=H/log⁡k∈[0,1]H_{\text{norm}}=H/\log k\in[0,1], so that entropy is comparable across different values of kk.

3.2 Token-level confidence

Following the Chow-style formalization of [7], we also record, as a complementary signal, each sample’s average per-token log-probability under the generating model (via compute_transition_scores), negated so that higher values indicate lower confidence: neg_logprob=−1T∑t=1TlogP(yt∣y<t)\text{neg\_logprob}=-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}) for the representative sample chosen from the majority cluster. This measures the model’s confidence in the tokens it actually produced, independent of whether other samples agreed with it – a different notion of uncertainty from semantic entropy, and one that can, in principle, catch cases where a model is consistently wrong (zero semantic entropy) but still assigns low probability to its own output.

3.3 Escalation labels and the three evaluation targets

For each query we compute correct_small and correct_large (exact-match or fuzzy alias match against ground truth, depending on task). Three binary targets can be constructed from these, which we refer to throughout as Targets 1–3:

Target 1: needs_escalation =(¬correct_small)∧correct_large,\displaystyle=(\lnot\,\text{correct\_small})\land\text{correct\_large}, (2)
Target 2: untrustworthy =¬correct_small,\displaystyle=\lnot\,\text{correct\_small}, (3)
Target 3: large_success =correct_large.\displaystyle=\text{correct\_large}. (4)

We initially evaluated signals only against Target 1, since it is the operationally relevant question (does escalating actually fix the answer?). However, Target 1 depends on the large model’s behavior, which a signal computed purely from the small model’s own samples never observes. We are careful to state this limitation precisely: such a signal carries no direct information about the large model, but it may still carry correlational information, mediated by a shared latent – query difficulty – that influences both models’ success. Fixed, parameter-free statistics such as entropy exploit this correlational pathway weakly, whereas a learned probe on internal representations can exploit it substantially better (Section 6.7). Target 2 is the target a per-model uncertainty signal can fairly be judged against, since it only requires information the small model’s own behavior could in principle encode.

Target 3 (defined above) applies to any signal, live or retrieval-based, but the two differ in what they can be expected to achieve against it: a live small-model signal has only indirect, difficulty-mediated access to the large model’s behavior (Section 6.5 shows this is nonzero but modest), whereas a knowledge base built by profiling queries against the large model (Section 7) has direct access to real correct_large outcomes. We report Targets 1 and 2 throughout and add Target 3 wherever a signal has something to say about it, and argue in Section 6.6 that this distinction resolves an apparent contradiction in our results.

A note on Target 3’s polarity, since it differs by signal family and is easy to misread. Entropy-family signals (semantic entropy, token confidence) are uncertainty scores: a higher value is designed to indicate trouble, uniformly across Targets 1 and 2. To preserve that reading for Target 3 as well, Tables 2 and 7 score these signals against ¬correct_large\lnot\text{correct\_large} rather than against correct_large as defined above – without this inversion, a higher-is-better entropy score would correspond to an AUROC read as 1−AUROC1-\text{AUROC} under the literal definition, inviting exactly the kind of misreading this note exists to prevent. Retrieval-based signals (Section 7) are different in kind: they vote directly on the outcome rather than report uncertainty, so a higher score naturally means predicted success, and Table 9 scores them against correct_large directly, matching the definition above without inversion. The two conventions are each the correct one for their own signal family; neither table is in error, but a reader comparing Target 3 AUROC values across both kinds of signal should note that they are scored against opposite classes.

3.4 Cost model

Every query incurs the cost of the kk-sample small-model pass, normalized to 11 unit (this is unavoidable, since the entropy signal requires it). Escalated queries additionally incur cost_ratio units for one large-model call. For escalation rate rr (fraction of queries escalated) and cost ratio ρ\rho,

cost​(r)=1+ρ⋅r.\text{cost}(r)=1+\rho\cdot r. (5)

We compare routed accuracy at a given cost against three baselines: always-small (cost 11), always-large (cost 1+ρ1+\rho), and random-at-matched-cost (escalate a random subset of the same size r⋅nr\cdot n, averaged over 20 trials) – the last of these isolates whether the signal’s escalation choices are actually better than an equal-cost random policy, rather than merely benefiting from escalating more often. We also compare against an oracle, in the spirit of the abstention framework of [11]: a hypothetical router that always makes the correct escalate-or-not decision. Its accuracy is capped by how many queries the small model already answers correctly that the large model would get wrong, since those are the only queries where escalating can actively hurt. This gives a cheap pre-flight check: an oracle’s margin over always-large bounds what any router, however good its signal, could possibly gain, so a small margin means a benchmark is not worth a full evaluation.

3.5 The sampling overhead this cost model hides

Normalizing the kk-sample pass to one unit obscures a constraint that turns out to bind hard in practice: entropy routing must draw kk generations from the small model before it can decide anything, and it pays that cost on every query, including the ones it does not escalate. Charging per generation instead, with a large-model generation costing γ\gamma times a small-model one,

costrouter=k+r​γ,costalways-large=γ,\text{cost}_{\text{router}}=k+r\gamma,\qquad\text{cost}_{\text{always-large}}=\gamma, (6)

so routing is cheaper than simply always calling the large model only when

γ>k1−r.\gamma>\frac{k}{1-r}. (7)

At k=10k=10 this requires γ>11.1\gamma>11.1 even at a 10%10\% escalation rate, and γ>14.3\gamma>14.3 at 30%30\%. The consequence is that the method’s viability depends on the model pair, not only on signal quality: a 270M/12B pair (∼\sim44×\times parameters) plausibly clears the bar, whereas the 1B/12B pair used in Section 6.4 (∼\sim12×\times) does not, and for that pair entropy routing is more expensive than always-large no matter how well the signal discriminates. We note this because it is easy to miss under a normalized cost model, and because it bounds the practical claim this line of work can make: semantic-entropy routing is only economically sensible at large capability (and hence large cost) ratios, or at substantially smaller kk than we use here. In Section 7, we propose an offline method based on retrieval to make the complexity argument above more appealing for real-world applications.

3.6 The difficulty baseline: a necessary control

An escalation signal is only interesting if it beats what is already known about the query for free. We therefore score, alongside every signal, a baseline that uses the benchmark’s own ground-truth difficulty as the routing score.

This baseline is a control, not a candidate router. Its role is the same as the oracle row in a Pareto table: an oracle is not deployable either, but it bounds what any router could achieve, and a signal approaching it means something. The question the difficulty baseline answers is diagnostic – does this signal carry information beyond how hard the question is? – and that question needs an answer whether or not difficulty happens to be available at inference. If the answer is no, one should build a cheap difficulty estimator rather than pay for kk samples and NLI inference.

Whether the baseline is additionally a deployable alternative depends on where its difficulty annotation comes from, and this varies sharply across our benchmarks (Table 1). Two regimes must be distinguished:

  • •

    When difficulty is a surface feature of the question – as on our synthetic arithmetic ladder, where it is operand digit count times operation count and a regex recovers it exactly – the baseline is a genuine zero-cost competitor. A signal that does not beat it provides no value, because the same routing decisions are available without any model call at all.

  • •

    When difficulty is latent – derived from the reference answer (GSM8K’s reasoning-step count) or requiring an external lookup (PopQA’s entity popularity) – the baseline is instead a skyline: it uses information unavailable at inference, since knowing how many reasoning steps a problem takes presupposes the solution one is trying to obtain. Beating it is then a strong result rather than a null one.

This control is cheap and, in our experience, decisive: it converted our strongest synthetic result from a positive finding into a null one (Section 6.5), and it is what distinguishes that null from the genuine GSM8K result (Section 6.1). We recommend it be reported by default. Its absence is, we suspect, why difficulty-correlated signals are easy to over-credit: any signal that tracks difficulty will separate a difficulty-driven target, whether or not it contains query-specific information.

We report two variants of this baseline, and recommend taking the larger of the two as the bar a signal must clear. The distinction turns on an assumption that scoring difficulty directly makes silently.

The raw baseline assumes the target is monotone in difficulty.

AUROC measures ranking quality, so using difficulty itself as the routing score asserts that higher difficulty implies a higher probability of the positive label. Where that assumption fails, the baseline scores poorly even when difficulty is highly informative, and a signal compared only against it can appear to add information it does not have.

Target 1 is the clearest case, because its positives are concentrated in the middle of the difficulty range rather than at the top. Writing the three regimes out:

Difficulty correct_small correct_large Target 1
low yes yes negative
medium no yes positive
high no no negative

Escalation helps only where the small model has failed and the large model succeeds. At low difficulty the small model is already correct; at high difficulty both fail. So P⁡(Target 1∣difficulty)P(\text{Target 1}\mid\text{difficulty}) is single-peaked, and ranking by raw difficulty places the hardest items – which are negatives – at the top. The ranking is not merely uninformative but wrong at precisely the end that a router acts on. Empirically this is what we observe: raw difficulty scores 0.5220.522 against Target 1 on GSM8K (Table 2), indistinguishable from chance, despite difficulty plainly bearing on whether escalation helps.

The calibrated baseline estimates the shape instead of assuming it.

Rather than scoring difficulty, we score the empirical rate of the target among items of similar difficulty, computed leave-one-out: for each item, we take its nearest neighbors in difficulty among the remaining items and use the fraction of them that are positive. This estimates P⁡(label∣difficulty)P(\text{label}\mid\text{difficulty}) nonparametrically, so a single-peaked relationship is represented correctly – medium-difficulty items receive high scores, and both tails receive low ones. The leave-one-out construction is necessary rather than fastidious: including an item’s own label in its own score would make the score partly be the label.

Concretely, the neighbor count is fixed at 88, not chosen by cross-validation: for each item we first collect every other item at the exact same difficulty value, and fall back to the 88 nearest by absolute difficulty distance only when fewer than 88 exact matches exist. This favors exact-match neighbors where the benchmark’s difficulty levels are discrete enough to supply them (as on the synthetic ladder), and degrades gracefully to a fixed-radius nearest-neighbor estimate otherwise (as on GSM8K, where difficulty values are less repetitive).

The size of this effect is not merely theoretical, but we are careful here to cite only what we can verify. Target 1 is single-peaked by the argument above on every benchmark we test, and raw difficulty scores accordingly poorly against it throughout: 0.5220.522 on GSM8K (Table 2), 0.5170.517–0.5600.560 across GSM8K’s own kk-ablation samples (Table 5), and 0.5590.559–0.5630.563 on the synthetic benchmark (Table 7) – all indistinguishable from chance. We do not, however, have a verified instance in our own data of the calibrated variant turning this into a large gain on Target 1 specifically – GSM8K’s calibrated score (0.4990.499, Table 2) is if anything slightly worse than raw there, consistent with our later point that calibration helps only when the benchmark’s difficulty annotation itself correlates with outcomes, which GSM8K’s reasoning-step count does weakly at best. The clearest demonstrated instance of calibration recovering non-monotone structure in this paper is therefore the raw-difficulty failure itself, not a specific calibrated figure we can point to: a baseline that scores nothing against Target 1’s non-monotone shape would need calibration to express it at all, even where we cannot yet show by how much.

Neither variant dominates.

Calibration is not free: it estimates a rate from a handful of neighbors, and that estimate is noisy. Where the relationship genuinely is monotone, raw difficulty already expresses it exactly and calibration can only perturb the ordering. GSM8K Target 2 illustrates this – ¬\lnotcorrect_small rises monotonically with difficulty, and raw difficulty (0.6490.649) accordingly beats the calibrated variant (0.5580.558), which is estimating a shape that was not in doubt. The two variants are thus complementary: calibration recovers structure the raw form cannot express, and the raw form avoids estimation noise the calibrated form incurs. Reporting only one invites a signal to clear whichever bar happens to be lower on that dataset, which is why we take the maximum.

An asymmetry worth stating.

The calibrated baseline consumes other items’ labels, whereas semantic entropy observes none. It is therefore a fair comparator for retrieval-based routers – a nearest-neighbor vote over cached outcomes is itself a calibrated conditional estimate, so scoring such a router against raw difficulty alone systematically overstates it (Section 7) – and a deliberately harsh one for live signals. Semantic entropy exceeding it by +0.313+0.313 on GSM8K Target 2 is correspondingly stronger evidence than the margin alone conveys, since it is outperforming a predictor granted information the signal itself never receives.

3.7 Harmful and wasted escalation

Beyond aggregate accuracy, we track two per-escalation diagnostics. Both are post-hoc evaluation quantities: they require ground-truth grading of both models and are therefore not computable at deployment time, but they characterize the failure modes a routing policy incurs in a way aggregate accuracy obscures:

harmful =P⁡(correct_small∧¬correct_large∣escalated),\displaystyle=P(\text{correct\_small}\land\lnot\,\text{correct\_large}\mid\text{escalated}), (8)
wasted =P⁡(correct_small∣escalated).\displaystyle=P(\text{correct\_small}\mid\text{escalated}). (9)

harmful captures the worst outcome – escalation actively breaking a correct answer; wasted captures the broader cost of escalating when the small model was already adequate, regardless of what the large model does.

4 Implementation

The pipeline consists of an inference module (InferenceEngine, wrapping any HuggingFace causal LM, generating kk samples with optional per-token log-probabilities), a semantic-entropy module (NLIEntailmentChecker and SemanticEntropyEstimator, implementing the clustering and entropy computation above), an answer-extraction module (AnswerExtractor, reducing a raw generation to a terse final answer via numeric extraction or last-sentence extraction before clustering), a router (Router, implementing the threshold escalation policy end to end), and an evaluation harness (evaluate.py) tying all of the above together across five benchmark loaders (synthetic arithmetic, GSM8K [14], PopQA [3], TriviaQA [15], TruthfulQA [16]) with a pre-flight sanity check and full AUROC/AUPRC/Pareto reporting. This paper reports results on three of the five (synthetic arithmetic, GSM8K, PopQA); TriviaQA and TruthfulQA loaders exist in the harness but were not run for this study.

4.1 Experimental settings

Unless stated otherwise, all runs use k=10k=10 samples per query, an NLI entailment threshold of τ=0.5\tau=0.5, a maximum generation length of 256 new tokens (raised from an initial 128 to accommodate chain-of-thought reasoning; see Section 5), and nucleus sampling [18] at temperature 0.70.7 with top-​p=0.95\text{top-}p=0.95 and top-​k=50\text{top-}k=50. Stochastic sampling is required rather than optional: greedy decoding would return kk identical samples and yield zero entropy regardless of the model’s true uncertainty. Generation models are loaded in bfloat16; the NLI model (microsoft/deberta-large-mnli [17], ∼\sim400M parameters) is kept in float32 (Section 5). We later ablate the sample budget kk (Section 6.2); we did not perform a sensitivity analysis over τ\tau, which remains a natural candidate for ablation.

Costs are reported as escalation rate rather than in absolute units. This is without loss of generality: under the model of Section 3.4, a budget equal to fraction ff of always-large’s premium permits escalation rate r≤fr\leq f for any ρ\rho, since 1+ρ​r≤1+f​ρ⇔r≤f1+\rho r\leq 1+f\rho\iff r\leq f. The cost ratio is thus a units conversion rather than a free parameter, and no sensitivity analysis over it is meaningful.

Reproducibility.

All runs were executed on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. The kk-sample ablation of Section 6.2 used a fixed seed (00) for item selection across k∈{3,5,10}k\in\{3,5,10\}, so item selection did not vary across that ablation; the generations themselves are stochastic (temperature 0.70.7) and are not separately seeded, which is the source of the run-to-run variance discussed in Section 6.5. From the timestamps recorded in our run logs, consecutive 250250-item GSM8K runs at this kk range completed roughly 7575–8080 minutes apart; we report this as an approximate, retrospective interval between logged runs rather than a controlled timing measurement, since other processes may have run on the same hardware between them. Seed values for the GSM8K replication sample and the 9696-item synthetic re-analysis (Sections 6.1 and 6.5) were not separately recorded beyond noting that they used a different or disjoint seed from the primary run; we report this limitation rather than reconstruct specific values we do not have.

5 Debugging Log: Real Failure Modes Encountered

Several non-obvious implementation issues surfaced during development, each of which would silently distort results if left unfixed. We record them here since they recurred across the project and are not specific to any one experiment.

Stylistic-elaboration confound.

Early raw-generation clustering conflated genuine disagreement with stylistic embellishment: for the query “What is the capital of Australia?”, several samples correctly named Canberra but appended fabricated tangential details (wrong region, invented history, fictitious statistics). Bidirectional entailment correctly failed on these pairs – the longer answer’s extra claims are not entailed by the short answer – inflating entropy to near-maximum (Hnorm=1.0H_{\text{norm}}=1.0) despite near-unanimous agreement on the actual answer. This motivated AnswerExtractor, which clusters a terse extracted answer instead of the raw generation.

NLI question-context suppression.

Wrapping each answer in a "Question: … Answer: …" template before the NLI check – intended to disambiguate short answers – turned out to be out-of-distribution for a general-purpose MNLI checkpoint, systematically suppressing entailment probabilities and inflating entropy even for textually near-identical answers. Disabling this wrapper by default resolved the issue; it is now opt-in.

dtype mismatch on the NLI model.

Loading the NLI model in bfloat16 (to save memory) produced a RuntimeError inside DeBERTa’s disentangled-attention matmul, since some internal buffers do not consistently cast across backends. The fix is to keep the (small, ∼\sim400M-parameter) NLI model in float32 while using bfloat16 only for the (much larger) generation models, where the memory savings matter.

OOM during model loading.

Instantiating models with the library default (float32, without low_cpu_mem_usage) caused a transient peak roughly double the model’s steady-state memory footprint during the loading step itself, triggering an OOM kill even on hardware that could otherwise hold the model comfortably. Setting low_cpu_mem_usage=True and defaulting to bfloat16 resolved this.

Prompt-induced capability-gap suppression.

An early arithmetic prompt (“Answer with just the final number”) forced single-shot mental arithmetic with no scratchpad, for both models. At higher difficulty (multi-digit, multi-step expressions), this erased most of a larger model’s real advantage, which stems substantially from chain-of-thought reasoning (carrying digits, tracking intermediate sums). The small and large models then performed similarly poorly, which superficially resembled “the large model is too weak” but was actually an artifact of a prompt that suppressed the mechanism by which model scale helps on this task. Allowing reasoning (“Show your work step by step, then state the final answer”) and extracting only the last number for grading resolved this.

Lone-surrogate Unicode crash.

Generation occasionally produced invalid UTF-8 (a lone surrogate character), typically when max_new_tokens truncated output mid-multi-byte-character. This crashed CSV serialization at the very end of a full run. Sanitizing decoded text immediately after generation (encode(..., errors="replace").decode(...)) fixes this at the source.

Small-sample AUROC instability.

A promising result at n=15n=15 (semantic-entropy AUROC against needs_escalation of 0.6020.602–0.6300.630 for the combined signal) did not replicate at n=100n=100 on the same benchmark family (AUROC collapsed to 0.500.50–0.530.53, chance level), despite the larger run having a more favorable escalation-worthy population by every other measure. We return to this in Section 6.5.

6 Results

We open with the two benchmarks side by side, because the contrast between them is the result. Semantic entropy posts a strong-looking score on both; on one it survives the controls of Section 3.6 and on the other it does not, and no number visible without those controls distinguishes the two cases. Sections 6.4 and 6.5 then give the failing benchmarks in full, which is where most of the methodological content lies.

6.1 Two benchmarks, one signal, opposite verdicts

The synthetic benchmark first, because it is the cautionary case.

Our initial experiments used a synthetic chained-arithmetic ladder with difficulty controlled by operand digit count and operation count. On it, semantic entropy separates the fair target (¬\lnotcorrect_small) at AUROC 0.8300.830 and 0.8670.867 across two profiling runs – figures we accepted as a positive result. Applying the difficulty baseline of Section 3.6 withdraws it. Scoring the benchmark’s own difficulty directly, which on this ladder a regular expression recovers from the question text at no cost, gives 0.8390.839 and 0.8300.830: a tie, with the sign of the difference flipping between runs and both gaps inside the 0.040.04 noise floor. Ten stochastic generations and NLI clustering purchase no routing decisions a regex does not already supply. A second precondition fails independently – oracle headroom over always-large is only +0.021+0.021, so even a perfect router had almost nothing to win. Section 6.5 gives the full analysis; what matters here is that neither failure is visible in the 0.8300.830 itself.

GSM8K, where the same signal survives the same controls.

We evaluated a Gemma-3 1B (small) / 12B (large) pair [20] on n=250n=250 GSM8K [14] items with k=10k=10 samples per query. This configuration passes the headroom precondition that synthetic arithmetic failed: always-small accuracy 0.3720.372, always-large 0.4840.484, and oracle 0.5720.572, leaving +0.088+0.088 of accuracy headroom – four times what the synthetic ladder offered. The both-wrong population is 0.4280.428.

Three things stand out. First, semantic entropy separates Target 2 at 0.8710.871, an interval well clear of chance, and the operationally relevant Target 1 at 0.7340.734 – substantially better than the 0.6130.613 and 0.6660.666 the same signal managed on synthetic arithmetic.

Second, and decisively, the comparison that withdrew the synthetic result confirms this one. Entropy beats raw difficulty by +0.212+0.212 on Target 1 and +0.222+0.222 on Target 2, and the harsher difficulty-calibrated baseline by +0.235+0.235 and +0.313+0.313, with disjoint confidence intervals on Target 2 ([0.820,0.915][0.820,0.915] vs. [0.486,0.629][0.486,0.629]). Where the synthetic gap was −0.009-0.009 and +0.037+0.037 – inside the noise floor, with the sign unstable – these margins exceed it by a factor of five and hold in the same direction across both baselines. The two benchmarks are separated not by the raw AUROC, which is comparable (0.8300.830 against 0.8710.871), but entirely by the margin over what difficulty already explains. Entropy carries query-specific information here and did not there.

It is worth being precise about what the baseline had access to on this benchmark, because it strengthens the claim. GSM8K ships no difficulty label, so we approximate difficulty by the number of calculation lines in the reference solution (Section 3.6). That quantity is derived from the answer: knowing how many reasoning steps a problem requires presupposes having solved it. The difficulty baseline on GSM8K is therefore a skyline rather than a deployable competitor, and semantic entropy – which observes only the small model’s own samples, and no labels at all – outperforms a predictor that was permitted to inspect the ground-truth solution. The calibrated variant is stronger still in this respect, since it additionally consumes other items’ outcome labels. A signal beating both is doing something neither difficulty nor difficulty-conditioned outcome frequency can do: distinguishing between two problems that require the same number of steps.

Note that on GSM8K the calibrated baseline is weaker than raw difficulty (0.5580.558 vs. 0.6490.649 on Target 2), the reverse of what we observe on synthetic arithmetic. The two baselines are not ordered in general: calibration estimates P⁡(label∣difficulty)P(\text{label}\mid\text{difficulty}) from a handful of same-difficulty neighbors, which recovers non-monotonic structure that raw difficulty cannot express, but injects estimation noise where the relationship is monotone and neighbors are few. GSM8K’s difficulty annotation correlates only weakly with outcomes (ρ=0.319\rho=0.319 for entropy against difficulty, versus 0.6570.657 on synthetic), so calibration costs more than it recovers. We therefore recommend reporting both and treating the maximum as the bar a signal must clear.

Third, Target 3 is the exception: entropy (0.6390.639) and raw difficulty (0.6330.633) are indistinguishable, though entropy does beat the calibrated variant (0.5350.535). This is consistent with the structural argument of Section 3.3 – whatever a small-model-only signal knows about the large model’s success appears to be mediated by shared query difficulty, with little additional query-specific contribution.

Routing performance.

The signal converts into real routing gains (Table 3). Accuracy exceeds the random-at-matched-cost baseline at every operating point above a 4%4\% escalation rate, peaking at +0.093+0.093, and exceeds always-large accuracy for escalation rates between roughly 0.370.37 and 0.890.89 – that is, the router is not merely approximating the large model more cheaply, it is outperforming it, by declining to escalate items the large model would have gotten wrong.

Replication on an independent sample.

The knowledge-base experiment of Section 7 incidentally profiles a second, disjoint GSM8K sample with the same model pair (n=150n=150, drawn with a different seed), which we can score with the same signals. It replicates the result above (Table 4). On Target 2 the two runs agree to within 0.0080.008 AUROC – a fifth of the ≈0.04\approx 0.04 noise floor of Section 6.5, and notably tighter than that floor despite being a harder test, since the floor is measured across re-samplings of a fixed item set whereas these two runs draw different items. Entropy’s margin over the stronger difficulty baseline is +0.222+0.222 and +0.242+0.242 respectively. Target 1 differs more (0.7340.734 vs. 0.6480.648), which at these sample sizes we do not regard as resolvable: the two intervals overlap substantially. The intervals also show the two targets to be on different footings. On Target 2, entropy’s interval is disjoint from both difficulty baselines’ in both samples, so the margin is not a sampling artifact. On Target 1 that separation holds only in the larger sample; at n=150n=150 entropy’s interval ([0.549,0.743][0.549,0.743]) overlaps raw difficulty’s ([0.414,0.607][0.414,0.607]), so the Target 1 margin should be read as directional rather than established.

Token confidence is not universally anti-informative.

On GSM8K, neg-logprob reaches 0.6480.648/0.6470.647 on Targets 1 and 2 – weak but clearly above chance – and fusing it with entropy improves Target 1 (0.7490.749 vs. 0.7340.734). This directly contradicts what we observed on synthetic arithmetic, where the same signal was below chance and fusion degraded entropy (Section 6.5). We take this as evidence that the earlier inversion was a property of that benchmark rather than of token confidence in general, and as a caution against generalizing fusion results across datasets.

The cost case does not close, and the reason is structural.

The accuracy result above does not by itself make this configuration deployable. Under the per-generation accounting of Section 3.5, routing at the best operating point (r=0.56r=0.56) is cheaper than always-large only if the large model costs more than k/(1−r)≈23k/(1-r)\approx 23 times a small-model generation. A 1B/12B pair is roughly 12×12\times by parameter count, so in absolute terms the policy costs k+r​γ=16.7k+r\gamma=16.7 units against always-large’s 1212: one would pay 39%39\% more than calling the large model on every query. We use parameter count as a proxy for γ\gamma throughout this paper; real serving cost also depends on batching, quantization, KV-cache bandwidth, and hardware, none of which parameter count captures, and a measured cost ratio from an actual serving stack would be a stronger basis for this argument than the proxy we use here. This is the distinction the normalized cost model of Section 3.4 conceals, and it is worth reporting separately from signal quality.

The binding term is kk, not the routing. Semantic entropy needs kk complete generations before it can decide anything, so its overhead is fixed rather than proportional to the escalation rate, and no threshold choice removes it. Any remedy must therefore attack the sampling budget rather than the routing policy. Section 7 examines one such remedy, and quantifies what it costs in signal quality.

6.2 The sample budget: ablating kk

k=10k{=}10 fails the break-even condition of Eq. 7 (costs 1.38×1.38\times always-large). Re-running at k∈{3,5,10}k\in\{3,5,10\}: T2 AUROC is 0.791/0.865/0.8620.791/0.865/0.862 – k=5k{=}5 and k=10k{=}10 agree to 0.0030.003, an order of magnitude inside the noise floor, while k=3k{=}3 costs 0.0740.074. Always-small accuracy rises with kk too (0.312/0.364/0.3920.312/0.364/0.392), since the pipeline reports the majority-cluster answer, so kk doubles as a self-consistency ensemble. At k=5k{=}5, routing strictly dominates always-large: cost 9.809.80–11.611.6 units against always-large’s 12.012.0, at equal or better accuracy, versus k=10k{=}10’s 16.616.6 units (never competitive). The barrier we reported as a property of the method was a hyperparameter we had never varied. At k=3k{=}3, token confidence overtakes entropy on T1 (0.6580.658 vs. 0.6300.630) – entropy degrades with fewer samples, confidence does not, and their fusion’s advantage widens as kk shrinks.

Table 5 gives all three targets across k∈{3,5,10}k\in\{3,5,10\} underlying this summary; Target 3’s difficulty baseline is identical across all three rows (0.6330.633), an internal check that the item set did not change with kk. Table 6 gives the cost-accuracy frontier in full: at k=10k{=}10 no configuration dominates always-large, while four configurations at k≤5k\leq 5 do.

This ablation’s own k=10k{=}10 row (T1 0.6820.682, T2 0.8620.862, T3 0.6840.684) differs from Table 2’s headline k=10k{=}10 numbers (0.7340.734, 0.8710.871, 0.6390.639) for what is nominally the same configuration; T2’s gap (0.0090.009) sits inside the noise floor, but T1’s (0.0520.052) and T3’s (0.0450.045) exceed it. The same re-sampling also moves the majority-cluster vote itself: always-small accuracy reads 0.3920.392 here against 0.3720.372 in Table 2, and oracle headroom +0.112+0.112 against +0.088+0.088 – gaps of the same size and origin as the AUROC ones, since which answer wins the cluster vote is exactly what a fresh kk-sample draw can flip. Both runs share the same seed and item selection (confirmed from our run manifests) but draw independent stochastic samples at generation time, so all of this is the same run-to-run variance documented in Section 6.5 rather than a discrepancy between the two tables – the ablation was a fresh kk-sample run, not a re-scoring of the cached run behind Table 2.

6.3 Synthetic arithmetic: capability gap and prompt sensitivity

On a synthetic chained-arithmetic ladder (difficulty controlled via operand digit-count and operation count), a Qwen2.5-0.5B/Qwen2.5-7B pair [21] showed a real but narrow accuracy gap before the prompt fix described in Section 5, and a much larger gap afterward. Pre-flight checks (small sample of 10 items, 1 generation each) proved useful for catching two degenerate regimes before committing to a full kk-sample run: both models at floor accuracy (no headroom for any signal), and both models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy (no capability gap for escalation to exploit).

6.4 PopQA: escalation is the wrong intervention

PopQA proved unusable for this study, for a reason worth separating from ordinary experimental difficulty. Two effects had to be disentangled.

First, an extraction/grading mismatch was suppressing measured accuracy by roughly half. Our QA pipeline reduced each generation with a last_sentence extractor before grading it with a substring alias matcher. But the matcher is designed to find a short answer embedded in prose, so extracting the final clause first discards the text it was built to search: a response such as “George Rankin was a politician. He served in the Australian House of Representatives until 1949.” is graded incorrect, because the extracted final sentence omits the answer. Grading the raw generation instead raised Gemma-3 12B from 0.120.12 to 0.280.28 and 1B from 0.040.04 to 0.120.12 on matched pre-flight samples. This is a genuine interaction bug between two individually correct components, and it is silent: it presents as uniformly weak models rather than as an error.

Second, and decisively, the corrected numbers still leave 72%72\% of items wrong for both models, with zero pre-flight items on which the small model succeeded where the large one failed. The dominant failure mode on long-tail PopQA is not small-model uncertainty but absent parametric knowledge in both models, exactly as the dataset’s design rationale anticipates [3]. Escalation cannot repair an answer neither model knows; this is a retrieval problem wearing a routing problem’s clothing. We therefore regard PopQA as mis-specified for escalation research rather than as a negative result about semantic entropy, and note the general principle: a large small/large capability gap is not sufficient: what matters is whether the large model succeeds where the small one fails, which is a different quantity.

6.5 Synthetic arithmetic: three runs, and a null result once controlled

Section 6.1 gave the headline: on this benchmark a regular expression matches semantic entropy, and oracle headroom is +0.021+0.021. This section supplies the full analysis, and the history that produced it – we ran the ladder three times with Gemma small/large pairs, and the three runs gave three different impressions of the same signal. A 1515-item pilot showed semantic entropy separating the fair target almost perfectly (AUROC 0.9290.929, and 1.0001.000 for the entropy/token-confidence fusion) while looking weak against needs_escalation (0.6200.620). A 100100-item follow-up on the same benchmark family collapsed to chance against needs_escalation for every signal (0.500.50–0.530.53), with routed accuracy tracking the random-at-matched-cost baseline at every operating point of the Pareto sweep. Neither run carried confidence intervals, and neither was scored against a difficulty baseline.

Both are superseded by a properly powered re-analysis. The knowledge-base experiments of Section 7 profiled a 9696-item synthetic set twice, storing per-item entropy, token confidence, and both correctness labels; the entropy in each cached entry was computed by kk-sampling the small model at profiling time, so these are genuine live-signal measurements. The two runs share their item set and their model pair, and differ only in re-sampling: the greedily decoded large model returns identical labels, while the small model’s kk samples flip two of 9696 items. They therefore isolate the run-to-run variance of the pipeline itself, holding the data fixed. All figures carry 95%95\% percentile bootstrap intervals over 20002000 resamples (Table 7), and the raw difficulty baseline of Section 3.6 is reported. We omit the calibrated variant here, unlike on GSM8K: this benchmark’s difficulty is lexically recoverable by regex, so raw difficulty is already the genuine zero-cost deployable competitor the calibrated baseline exists to approximate elsewhere, and adding it would re-estimate a shape that is not in question on this benchmark rather than add a harsher bar.

Five findings follow, four of which revise claims made earlier in this paper.

The central claim strengthens.

Semantic entropy separates the fair target at AUROC 0.8300.830 and 0.8670.867, with both intervals excluding 0.50.5 by a wide margin, while performing far worse on Target 1 (0.6130.613, 0.6660.666). The target-choice effect is therefore not an artifact of the n=15n=15 pilot: it replicates at n=96n=96 with quantified uncertainty, and the gap between targets (≈0.2\approx 0.2 AUROC) exceeds the width attributable to sampling noise. The two runs also bound that noise directly, and do so in an unusually clean way: because they share their items and their model pair, entropy’s T2 AUROC differing by 0.0370.037 between them (0.8300.830 versus 0.8670.867) is attributable to kk-sampling stochasticity alone, with no contribution from which items happened to be drawn. This is the relevant quantity for interpreting a single run, and it implies that AUROC differences below roughly 0.040.04 in this setting should not be read as findings. We use 0.040.04 as a noise floor throughout, noting that it is measured at n=96n=96 and would be somewhat tighter at n=250n=250.

Token confidence is anti-informative, and the pilot figure does not replicate.

Token neg-logprob falls below chance in all four measurements, against both targets and in both datasets. The 0.8570.857 recorded for this signal against the fair target in the 1515-item pilot is not reproduced; at n=96n=96 the same signal scores 0.4310.431 and 0.4330.433. No individual interval here excludes 0.50.5, so we do not claim significant anti-correlation from any single measurement, but the consistency of the direction across four independent measurements makes chance an unattractive explanation. We treat the n=15n=15 figure as small-sample noise and recommend against reading it as evidence for token confidence as a routing signal.

The fusion question resolves.

Section 6.7 reported that fusing neg-logprob into the combined score hurt performance, and noted that we lacked a principled account of when fusion helps versus hurts. Table 7 supplies one for this setting: the fused component is itself anti-correlated with the target, so an equal-weight combination necessarily degrades entropy alone – as observed (0.7520.752 vs. 0.8300.830; 0.7590.759 vs. 0.8670.867). This is a property of the component signal, not an unexplained interaction. A plausible mechanism is a length confound: avg_neg_logprob averages surprise over tokens, and harder items elicit longer chain-of-thought containing more highly-predictable connective tokens, which lowers mean per-token surprise precisely where the answer is least reliable. We flag this as a hypothesis with a direct test (correlating the signal against ground-truth difficulty) rather than an established result.

Live entropy does predict large-model failure, contradicting our earlier claim.

On Target 3, live semantic entropy reaches AUROC 0.7220.722 and 0.7140.714, with both intervals excluding 0.50.5. Earlier sections of this paper asserted that a small-model-only signal carries no information about large-model behavior; that is too strong. The correlational pathway anticipated in Section 3.3 – shared query difficulty influencing both models – is not marginal but substantial, recovering most of the discrimination that cached large-model outcomes achieve (Section 7). The defensible claim is that retrieval predicts large-model success better, not that live sampling cannot do it at all.

The difficulty baseline eliminates the synthetic result entirely.

Applying the control of Section 3.6 to these datasets is decisive. Scoring the benchmark’s ground-truth difficulty directly as a routing signal gives Target 2 AUROC 0.8390.839 and 0.8300.830 – statistically indistinguishable from semantic entropy’s 0.8300.830 and 0.8670.867, with the sign of the difference flipping between the two datasets and both gaps falling inside the 0.040.04 noise floor established above. On Target 3 the baseline is better (0.7910.791 vs. 0.7220.722 and 0.7140.714), consistently across both runs.

The difficulty of an item on this benchmark is its operand digit count times its operation count, both readable from the question string by a regular expression. Ten stochastic generations and (102)\binom{10}{2} NLI entailment computations therefore purchase no routing decisions that a regex does not already supply. A supporting diagnostic makes the mechanism explicit: entropy’s rank correlation with difficulty is ρ=0.657\rho=0.657, while its Somers’ DD against the Target 2 label is 0.6600.660 – two different statistics that agree closely at n=96n=96, indicating that essentially all of its discriminative power on this benchmark is difficulty tracking rather than query-specific uncertainty.

We report this as a null result for the synthetic benchmark specifically, not for semantic entropy: on GSM8K the same signal beats the same baseline by +0.222+0.222 (Section 6.1). The lesson is about benchmark construction. A synthetic task with a parameterized difficulty ladder makes difficulty a surface feature of the input by design, which hands any difficulty-correlated signal an unearned result and makes the benchmark unable to distinguish a good uncertainty estimator from a difficulty regex. This failure is invisible without the control, and it coexisted in our data with the headroom failure described below – two independent reasons the same experiments could not have supported the conclusion we initially drew from them.

A precondition we should have checked first.

On these datasets the oracle router reaches 0.6770.677 against always-large’s 0.6560.656: a perfect router gains +0.021+0.021. Since an oracle escalates exactly when ¬correct_small∧correct_large\lnot\text{correct\_small}\land\text{correct\_large}, its accuracy is P⁡(correct_small∨correct_large)P(\text{correct\_small}\lor\text{correct\_large}) and its advantage over always-large is P⁡(correct_small∧¬correct_large)P(\text{correct\_small}\land\lnot\text{correct\_large}) – the items it protects by declining to escalate. When that quantity is small and the both-wrong population is large (0.3230.323 here), no router can demonstrate a useful win over always-large regardless of signal quality. This is a property of the benchmark rather than of any signal; it is independent of the small/large capability gap being large (it is, 0.3850.385 vs. 0.6560.656), and it should be verified before committing to a full evaluation. Our observed best margin over matched-cost random escalation is +0.070+0.070, at a 70%70\% escalation rate – which Equation 7 shows requires γ>33\gamma>33 to be worth paying for at all.

6.6 Why the two targets diverge

The central conceptual finding of this work is that needs_escalation is an unfair evaluation target for any signal computed solely from the small model’s own behavior. Consider the negative class (needs_escalation = false) in the n=100n=100 run: it contains both “small correct” items (naturally low entropy) and “both models wrong” items. The latter are, from the small model’s perspective, behaviorally indistinguishable from true escalation-worthy items – the small model is equally uncertain in both cases, because its uncertainty reflects its own difficulty with the query, not whether a specific other model would resolve that difficulty. When the “both wrong” subpopulation is large (as it was at n=100n=100, given always-large accuracy of only 0.360.36), it fills the same high-entropy region as the true positives, collapsing AUROC toward chance – not because the signal is uninformative, but because the label it is being scored against encodes a fact (large-model success) that is causally downstream of a different model entirely.

This reframing is consistent with the AUROC results throughout the paper: strong performance against Target 2 and weak performance against Target 1 throughout the synthetic runs of Section 6.5. The harm/waste diagnostics do not follow the same clean pattern across scales: they were near-zero at n=15n=15 but consistently nonzero at n=100n=100. This is expected rather than contradictory – these diagnostics measure the composition of the escalated set, which depends on the always-small accuracy and the size of the “both models wrong” population, and both differed substantially between the two runs. They are therefore not evidence for or against the target-choice argument, and we do not read them as such.

6.7 A learned alternative: the confidence-gated router

A companion codebase developed by the present authors, using an independent implementation, applied a proper train/calibration/test methodology (rather than a single full-dataset pass) and added a learned hidden-state probe on top of semantic entropy, trained directly on needs_escalation using the small model’s mid-layer hidden states (layers 8–16, ensembled, strongly ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized). Unlike the fixed signals in this paper, a learned probe can in principle pick up correlates of the large model’s likely success indirectly, to the extent such correlates are reflected in the small model’s internal representations (e.g. query type, topic, or difficulty features that correlate with the large model’s competence on this class of query, even though the small model cannot directly observe the large model’s behavior). On a 72-item synthetic-arithmetic benchmark with a Gemma-3 270M/4B pair [20], this raised AUROC against needs_escalation from a semantic-entropy baseline of 0.7330.733 to 0.8950.895 over the course of an iterative search (Table 8), and routed accuracy from 0.5770.577 to 0.6150.615 – approximately 80% of the oracle’s achievable gain over always-small, escalating only 30% of queries.

This result is compatible with, rather than contradictory to, the negative finding of Section 6.5: it demonstrates that a fixed, parameter-free signal cannot reliably predict needs_escalation at scale, but a signal with a learned component, explicitly trained against that exact label on internal model representations, can recover meaningful separation that entropy and log-probability alone cannot reach. The final iteration’s conformal calibration gate [23] adds a distribution-free coverage guarantee on the escalation decision rather than changing its ranking, which is why it leaves AUROC and ACC@30 unchanged from iteration 5 (Table 8).

Notably, this independently-implemented pipeline reported the same pattern under its original (pre-calibration-split) methodology: fusing neg-logprob into the combined score hurt performance relative to entropy alone, without the specific figures preserved for this run. This qualitatively corroborates our n=100n{=}100 observation that fusion did not help and, in one instance (Section 6.5, n=15n{=}15), showed the opposite. We do not yet have a principled account of when fusion helps versus hurts; the balance of evidence suggests it should be validated per dataset/model pair rather than assumed either way.

As explained in Section 3.5, the kk-sample overhead that live entropy routing pays before it can make any escalation decision can still be high. The next section proposes an approach based on knowledge-base retrieval that trades accuracy for cost.

7 Knowledge-Base Retrieval: A Complementary, Cheaper Signal

The signals evaluated so far all require live kk-sampling at inference time: generating kk completions from the small model, clustering them, and computing entropy per query. An alternative is to profile a held-out set of queries once with the full expensive pipeline (samples, clustering, entropy, and a live call to the large model to obtain ground truth), cache the results in a knowledge base, and at inference time retrieve the nn nearest cached neighbors by embedding similarity and vote – replacing k+1k{+}1 model calls per query with a single embedding call.

7.1 Mechanism and an early methodological hazard

Each cached entry stores its embedding, entropy statistics, and outcome labels (correct_small, correct_large, needs_escalation). At query time, a new item is embedded once, its nn nearest neighbors retrieved by cosine similarity, and a similarity-weighted vote over neighbors’ labels produces both an escalation score and a mean neighbor similarity, the latter serving as a built-in confidence/coverage check. This check proved essential in practice: two separate runs used a knowledge base built with one embedding model while querying with a different one, producing near-zero neighbor similarity (∼\sim0.01–0.03) and, in the worse case, AUROC below chance – an inversion, not merely noise. Both incidents were caught only because neighbor similarity collapsed to noise-level values; a runtime warning was subsequently added to flag this condition automatically.

7.2 A structural asymmetry between the two signals

Live semantic entropy is computed purely from the small model’s own samples and therefore carries no direct information about how the large model would behave on a new query. Knowledge-base retrieval is different: its cached neighbors carry real, ground-truth correct_large outcomes from build time, obtained precisely because the large model was called during profiling. Target 1 is therefore not equally hard for the two signals – retrieval has a direct channel to the quantity the label depends on, and live sampling has only an indirect one.

We initially stated this asymmetry more strongly, as live entropy being structurally unable to say anything about large-model behavior. The n=96n=96 measurements in Section 6.5 show that this was wrong: live entropy predicts large-model failure at AUROC 0.7220.722 and 0.7140.714, with intervals excluding chance, via the shared-difficulty pathway described in Section 3.3. Retrieval’s advantage is therefore quantitative rather than categorical, and the comparison below should be read in that light.

To isolate this capability directly, we evaluate against Target 3 (Section 3.3): correct_large alone, i.e. will the large model succeed on this query? We predict it via a similarity-weighted vote over neighbors’ cached correct_large labels. Live entropy has no analogous prediction for this target – it never touches the large model for a new query – so Target 3 is knowledge-base-only by definition.

7.3 Results: a weaker signal at a price the strong one cannot meet

We evaluated the same retrieval pipeline on two benchmarks. On synthetic arithmetic (n=60n=60, Gemma-3 270M small / 1B embedding / 12B large) the results appeared to confirm the asymmetry argument above. On GSM8K (n=100n=100 eval against a 150150-item knowledge base built with disjoint seeds, Gemma-3 1B/12B) one specific claim does not survive, while the broader case for retrieval survives in a different form (Table 9).

Target 3 collapses from 0.9080.908 to 0.5180.518.

On synthetic arithmetic, retrieval predicted large-model success almost as well as any signal in this paper; on GSM8K it is indistinguishable from chance. Target 1 reverses as well – live entropy now outperforms retrieval (0.6560.656 vs. 0.5700.570), the opposite of the synthetic ordering that originally motivated the asymmetry argument.

The collapse was predicted in advance, and identifies the mechanism.

Before running GSM8K we probed the synthetic knowledge base by predicting each cached item’s difficulty leave-one-out from its neighbors’ difficulty, using the same similarity-weighted vote the KB uses for outcomes. It recovered difficulty at Spearman ρ=0.986\rho=0.986 and 0.9810.981 across two datasets: on that benchmark, “nearest in embedding space” and “same difficulty” are the same relation. Retrieval there was difficulty lookup, and its apparent skill on Target 3 was the difficulty-calibrated estimate of P⁡(correct_large∣difficulty)P(\text{correct\_large}\mid\text{difficulty}) described in Section 3.6 – an estimate available, we showed, without any embedding at all.

GSM8K removes the mechanism. Its difficulty is the number of calculation lines in the reference solution (Section 3.6), a property of the answer rather than a lexical feature of the question, so no embedding of the question text can recover it the way digit-and-operator counts are recoverable on the synthetic ladder. Running the same probe on the GSM8K knowledge base confirms this directly: ρ=0.231\rho=0.231, against 0.980.98 on synthetic. The mechanism is therefore measured on both sides of the comparison rather than inferred from one. We regard this as the strongest argument in this paper for reporting the difficulty probe by default: the prediction was made before GSM8K was run, from a diagnostic requiring no model calls, and it correctly forecast the collapse of our own most attractive result.

Signal quality is not the only axis, and on this model pair it is not the binding one.

Read as a contest, Table 9 says live sampling wins on GSM8K. Read against the cost constraint left open in Section 6.1, it says something else. Live entropy must pay kk complete generations before it can decide anything, so at r=0.56r=0.56 and γ=12\gamma=12 it costs k+r​γ=16.7k+r\gamma=16.7 units against always-large’s 1212 – a routing policy more expensive than calling the large model every time, however good its signal. Retrieval replaces those kk generations with a single embedding forward pass costing ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, relaxing the break-even condition from γ>k/(1−r)\gamma>k/(1-r) to γ>ε/(1−r)\gamma>\varepsilon/(1-r) – from 2323 to under 11 – and bringing the per-query cost to ε+r​γ≈6.8\varepsilon+r\gamma\approx 6.8 units, 57%57\% of always-large rather than 139%139\%. Of the two, only retrieval is deployable at this model ratio (Table 10).

Retrieval’s 6.86.8-unit serving cost omits the one-time cost of building the knowledge base itself: profiling each of the 150150 GSM8K items requires the full expensive pipeline (kk small-model samples plus one large-model call for ground truth), at k+γ=10+12=22k+\gamma=10+12=22 units per item, or 150×22=3300150\times 22=3300 units total. This cost is amortized over every query the knowledge base subsequently serves, so it matters only in the volume-dependent sense of how many queries are needed before it is paid off. Against live sampling’s 16.716.7 units per query, retrieval’s total cost (3300+6.8​N3300+6.8N for NN queries) falls below live sampling’s (16.7​N16.7N) once N>3300/(16.7−6.8)≈333N>3300/(16.7-6.8)\approx 333 – after roughly 334334 queries, retrieval is cheaper in total, not just per query. Against always-large’s 12.012.0 units per query the crossover is later, at N>3300/(12.0−6.8)≈635N>3300/(12.0-6.8)\approx 635 queries, since always-large’s per-query cost is itself lower than live sampling’s. Below these volumes the build cost dominates and retrieval is not yet the cheaper option in aggregate, even though its marginal cost per additional query already is.

The last two rows are the comparison that matters for retrieval’s defense: at essentially identical cost (6.86.8 versus 6.76.7 units), retrieval supplies a signal of 0.6070.607 where random escalation supplies none. Whatever else is true of the knowledge base on this benchmark, it is not paying for nothing.

The difficulty baselines are not policies, and on GSM8K they are not buildable.

Retrieval’s Target 2 score (0.6070.607) essentially matches the difficulty-calibrated baseline (0.6060.606), and it would be natural to read that equivalence as a null result – as we did on synthetic arithmetic, where it was one. It is not one here, and the distinction is worth making carefully, because it determines whether the reader should conclude “use difficulty instead” or “difficulty is not on the menu.”

On the synthetic ladder, difficulty is operand digit count times operation count. A regular expression over the question string recovers it exactly, at no cost, before any model is called. There the baseline is a competitor: a router built on it could be deployed tomorrow, and a signal that merely matches it is redundant.

On GSM8K, difficulty is the number of calculation lines in the reference solution (Section 3.6). Obtaining it requires the solution – and a system that already possessed the solution would have no reason to route the query at all. The baseline is therefore circular as a policy: it consumes the very output the router exists to produce. The calibrated variant is more privileged still, since it additionally requires the graded outcomes of neighboring items, which is to say knowledge of whether the small model answered them correctly. Neither quantity is available at inference under any budget, which is why neither appears as a row in Table 10: they are not slower or more expensive alternatives, they are not alternatives.

What they remain is an upper bound – the accuracy a router could reach if difficulty were handed to it for free – and that is the role in which we use them throughout. A signal falling well short of the bound has room to improve; a signal matching it has extracted what difficulty affords. On this benchmark retrieval reaches that bound using only an embedding of the question, which is information a deployed system actually has. The correct reading of 0.6070.607 versus 0.6060.606 is therefore not that retrieval is redundant, but that it recovers, from the question alone, what an oracle with access to the reference solution and to neighboring items’ grades could achieve. That is a modest bound to reach – entropy exceeds it by a wide margin – but reaching it at 57%57\% of always-large’s cost is not nothing, and it is emphatically not the same finding as the synthetic null.

A frontier rather than a winner.

The honest summary is that the two methods occupy different points on a cost–quality frontier, and that neither dominates. Live sampling buys the strongest signal in this paper (0.8720.872 on Target 2) at a price this model pair cannot pay. Retrieval buys a weaker but real signal (0.6070.607) at 57%57\% of always-large’s cost. A practitioner at γ=12\gamma=12 has exactly one of these available; one at γ≥25\gamma\geq 25 has both, and should prefer live sampling. What we retract is not the value of retrieval but the specific claim that motivated it – that cached large-model outcomes give retrieval a capability live sampling structurally lacks. On the benchmark where difficulty is not lexically recoverable, that capability is absent.

The gap between 0.8720.872 and 0.6070.607 is, we think, the quantity worth attacking. It measures what is forfeited by declining to pay the kk-generation term. The learned probe of Section 6.7 is the natural candidate for closing it, since a forward pass over hidden states also avoids that term while retaining access to the model’s own computation on the specific query; Section 8 develops this and related directions.

One limitation is resolved, in retrieval’s favour.

We had noted that scoring the knowledge base on Target 2 using its escalation score – a vote over neighbors’ needs_escalation labels – might understate it, since live entropy is scored on its native quantity. Implementing a dedicated vote over neighbors’ ¬\lnotcorrect_small labels shows the concern is unfounded: 0.6070.607 versus 0.6050.605, a bias of +0.002+0.002 AUROC.

A caveat on thresholds.

On GSM8K the knowledge base’s binary escalation decisions, taken at the default score threshold of 0.50.5, are correct on 73%73\% of items – below the 80%80\% obtainable by never escalating at all, given Target 1’s prevalence of 0.2000.200. This is a statement about the threshold rather than the ranking: a signal with AUROC above chance can still produce a poor classifier at an arbitrary cut point, and at low prevalence accuracy rewards silence. Operating points should be selected from the Pareto curve as in Section 6.1, not inherited from a default, and threshold-free and thresholded metrics should both be reported.

7.4 Limitations of the retrieval result

The GSM8K result above supersedes the synthetic one, and resolves two of the three caveats we had attached to the latter. The Target 2 scoring concern is closed: a dedicated small-failure vote differs from the escalation score by +0.002+0.002 AUROC. The independence concern is closed by construction: the GSM8K knowledge base and evaluation set were drawn with different seeds, and we verify by question-string comparison that they are disjoint, so retrieval cannot match an item against itself.

Three limitations remain. First, both retrieval evaluations are single runs (n=60n=60 and n=100n=100) without repeated seeds, against a measured AUROC noise floor of ≈0.04\approx 0.04 (Section 6.5). The synthetic-to-GSM8K collapse on Target 3 (0.908 -> 0.518) is far too large to be noise, but the smaller GSM8K differences – Target 1’s 0.5700.570 versus 0.6560.656, for instance – are not individually resolvable at this precision.

Second, while the difficulty probe now confirms the mechanism on both benchmarks (ρ=0.98\rho=0.98 versus 0.2310.231), we have tested only two points on that axis. Whether retrieval degrades smoothly as lexical difficulty-salience decreases, or has a threshold, is unknown, and two benchmarks cannot distinguish those possibilities.

Third, the retrieval approach assumes queries arrive from a distribution the knowledge base covers, and neither benchmark tests the regime where that fails. On synthetic, mean neighbor similarity sat near 0.990.99 – the knowledge base had near-identical items to match against, which is closer to interpolation within a dense space than generalization to novel task types. Whether retrieval degrades gracefully or sharply under sparse coverage is untested, and matters more now that the mechanism we thought we had identified turns out not to be the one operating.

8 Future Work

8.1 Retrieval keys that encode failure, not surface form

The clearest direction this work points to is that the retrieval key is the wrong object. Our knowledge base embeds the question text with a general-purpose language model and retrieves by cosine similarity, which asks: what other questions look like this one? What a router actually needs is: what other questions does this model fail on in the same way? These coincide only when surface form happens to track failure – which is exactly the condition our difficulty probe measures, and exactly the condition that held on synthetic arithmetic (ρ=0.98\rho=0.98) and failed on GSM8K (ρ=0.23\rho=0.23). Read this way, the probe is not only a diagnostic for catching artifacts after the fact but an objective: a good retrieval key is one whose neighborhoods are predictive of outcomes, and the probe measures precisely that property, at no model cost, before any routing experiment is run. It can therefore be used to select or train keys prospectively. We see four candidate directions.

Learned keys trained on outcomes.

Rather than adopting an off-the-shelf embedding, one can train an encoder so that items with the same outcome are close and items with different outcomes are far apart – standard metric learning, with correct_small (or needs_escalation) as the supervision signal, over the same profiled corpus the knowledge base already requires. The profiling pass that builds the knowledge base yields exactly the labeled data this needs, so the training set is free once the knowledge base exists. The risk is overfitting a small corpus, and the appropriate check is the probe itself applied to a held-out split.

Keys drawn from the small model’s own state.

A question embedding describes the question; it does not describe what this model does when confronted with it. Two arithmetic problems of identical surface form can sit on opposite sides of a model’s competence boundary, and no encoder of the question text can separate them. The small model’s hidden states at the point of answering do carry that information – this is precisely why the learned probe of Section 6.7 outperforms fixed statistics – and they are obtainable from a single forward pass, preserving the cost advantage that makes retrieval viable (Section 7). Using hidden states as retrieval keys rather than as probe inputs would combine the two lines of work in this paper: the probe’s access to model-internal signal with retrieval’s access to cached large-model outcomes.

Explicit task-type and difficulty features.

Retrieval need not operate in a single undifferentiated space. Partitioning by task type first – arithmetic versus multi-hop factual versus commonsense – and retrieving within a partition would prevent the coverage failure we could not test (Section 7.4), where a novel task type matches nothing meaningful yet still returns confident neighbors. Cheap explicit features are also available and unexploited: quantity count, operation types, entity rarity, syntactic depth. On GSM8K these would not recover the answer-derived reasoning-step count, but they need not: they need only correlate with it well enough to make neighborhoods informative, and the probe provides a direct, zero-cost measure of whether a given feature set achieves that.

Hybrid keys using partial generation.

The kk-sampling cost that makes live entropy undeployable (Section 3.5) is driven by generating kk complete answers. Much of the signal may be available far earlier – from a single sample, from the first few tokens of kk samples, or from the entropy of the first branch point – at a fraction of the cost. A key combining a question embedding with a short prefix of the model’s own attempted answer would sit between the two extremes we tested, and the break-even analysis of Equation 7 gives an explicit budget for how much such a prefix may cost before the advantage over live sampling is lost.

8.2 Closing the signal gap

The gap between live entropy and retrieval on GSM8K (0.8720.872 versus 0.6070.607 on Target 2) quantifies what is lost by refusing to pay the kk-generation term, and is the natural target for the above. A useful intermediate result would be to establish whether that gap is a property of the key (in which case better keys close it) or of the information (in which case no question-side representation suffices, and only model-internal or partial-generation signals can help). The probe distinguishes these: if a learned key raises outcome-predictiveness substantially while routing performance does not follow, the limitation is informational rather than representational.

8.3 Ablations and validation we did not run

Two parameters were fixed throughout and never varied: sampling temperature (0.70.7), which directly determines the sample diversity semantic entropy measures and is therefore the most consequential remaining omission; and the NLI entailment threshold τ=0.5\tau=0.5. We did ablate the sample count kk (Section 6.2); both remaining parameters admit cheap sensitivity analyses on the existing pipeline.
