Separately, and more concretely: the knowledge-base profiling runs behind Table 9 and Table 10 did not preserve per-item scores, so the AUROC figures there – including the 0.908→0.5180.908\to 0.518 Target 3 collapse – carry no bootstrap interval, unlike this paper’s other live-signal AUROC results, which do (the deterministic difficulty baselines and the exploratory synth72 search log of Section 6.7 are reported as point estimates for unrelated reasons and were never bootstrapped either). Re-running that profiling pass with per-item scores retained, so a 95%95\% bootstrap interval can be computed the same way as elsewhere in this paper, is a concrete, low-cost next step rather than an open research question, and we list it here as such rather than let it pass as an unexplained gap (see also the Limitations paragraph in Section 9).

Our positive result also rests on one dataset and one model pair. It replicates across two disjoint GSM8K samples, but whether it transfers to another reasoning family, or to a model pair with a different competence relationship, is untested – and the reversals documented in Section 9 give ample reason not to assume it does. Finally, the mechanism relating embedding–difficulty correlation to retrieval performance rests on two points (ρ=0.98\rho=0.98 and 0.230.23); whether degradation between them is smooth or threshold-like is unknown, and a benchmark of intermediate lexical difficulty-salience would settle it.

8.4 Beyond a fixed kk, a single pair, and a binary decision

Several of this paper’s design choices were fixed for tractability rather than because they are the right choice in general, and each suggests a direction we did not pursue.

Adaptive sample budgets. We use a fixed kk for every query (ablated in Section 6.2, but still fixed within any one configuration). Most of the kk-sample cost is spent on queries where the small model’s samples agree quickly; an adaptive scheme that samples until a stopping criterion is met – or until the running entropy estimate stabilizes – would spend the budget only on genuinely ambiguous queries, potentially closing much of the gap in Section 3.5 without the fixed-kk cost on easy queries.

A three-way decision. Our router chooses between answer-with-small and escalate-to-large. A middle option – decline to answer at all – is standard in selective prediction [11] and would let the router abstain on queries where neither model is likely to be right (the both-wrong population that collapses several of this paper’s targets toward chance, Section 6.6), rather than being forced to pick one of two models that both fail.

Multi-tier cascades. We test a single small/large pair throughout. A cascade with more than two tiers would let a query escalate incrementally, and the oracle-headroom and cost-overhead arguments of this paper apply at each tier boundary, not just once.

Router portability. We do not test whether a router (fixed-threshold or learned) trained for one small/large pair transfers when either model is swapped for a different one of similar capability. If it does not, a router’s practical cost includes retraining for every model-pair change, which the cost accounting in this paper does not charge for.

A self-updating knowledge base. Section 7’s knowledge base is a fixed, one-time profiling pass over 150150 items. A deployed system would instead see a stream of queries it could profile continuously, growing the knowledge base and plausibly improving its coverage and the validity of the difficulty-probe diagnostic over time rather than leaving both fixed at their initial values.

9 Discussion

Semantic entropy is a usable escalation signal, but establishing that took three benchmarks and the repeated discovery that our own positive results were artifacts. A fourth check corroborates the same conclusion under a different method: an independently implemented confidence-gated probe, trained on a separate 72-item synthetic benchmark (Section 6.7), recovered most of the achievable gain over always-small using semantic entropy as its base signal. The generalisable content of this paper is the set of controls that separated the two.

Report the target explicitly.

Target 1 (does escalation help) and Target 2 (is the small model wrong) differ by more than 0.20.2 AUROC on identical data. A signal computed from the small model’s samples has only indirect access to the large model’s behavior, mediated by shared query difficulty – substantial, as Target 3 shows (0.720.72 on synthetic), but not the same thing as observing the large model. Papers that report one target without naming it are not comparable to each other.

Report a difficulty baseline.

This is the control we most regret omitting. On synthetic arithmetic a regex over the question matched semantic entropy exactly, converting our strongest result into a null one; on GSM8K entropy beats the same baseline by +0.222+0.222 and the result stands. The two cases are indistinguishable without the baseline. Any signal correlated with difficulty will separate a difficulty-driven target, so the question is never “does the signal work” but “does it beat what the question text already tells you.”

Check headroom before spending compute.

A benchmark can exhibit a wide capability gap and still leave a perfect router +0.021+0.021 over always-large, because the relevant quantity is P⁡(correct_small∧¬correct_large)P(\text{correct\_small}\land\lnot\text{correct\_large}) – how often the small model is right where the large model is wrong – not the accuracy difference between the models. On PopQA that quantity was zero. This is a cheap pre-flight computation and it invalidates entire experiments.

Cost the sampling overhead honestly.

Normalizing the kk-sample pass to one unit hides that entropy routing pays kk generations on every query before deciding anything. Under per-generation accounting the method saves money only when γ>k/(1−r)\gamma>k/(1-r), which at k=10k=10 demands a large model more than 11×11\times the per-generation cost of the small one even at a 10%10\% escalation rate. Our GSM8K configuration wins on accuracy and loses on cost – both worth reporting, and the second invisible under the normalized model.

On generalizing across datasets.

Three of our findings reversed between benchmarks, which is the most uncomfortable result in this paper. Token confidence was below chance on synthetic arithmetic and above it on GSM8K; fusing it degraded entropy in the first case and improved Target 1 in the second; and retrieval-based prediction of large-model success went from 0.9080.908 to chance. In each case the single-benchmark result would have been reported as a property of the signal. We now think it should not be: a signal’s behavior here is a joint property of the signal and the benchmark’s structure, and claims of the form “signal XX predicts YY” should be accompanied by the controls that establish which of the two is doing the work.

The retrieval case is the one where we can say what the benchmark contributed. Its difficulty was lexically recoverable, embedding similarity therefore encoded difficulty, and neighbor voting reduced to difficulty-conditioned outcome frequency – an estimator our own difficulty-calibrated baseline computes without any embedding. That the probe forecast the collapse before we ran GSM8K is, to us, the clearest argument for reporting these controls by default.

Limitations.

Our positive result rests on one dataset and one model pair. It does replicate across two disjoint samples of that dataset (n=250n=250 and n=150n=150, agreeing to 0.0080.008 AUROC on Target 2), but two samples from GSM8K are not two datasets, and nothing here establishes that the result transfers to another task family or another model pair. Sampling temperature was fixed at 0.70.7 throughout and never ablated, despite directly setting the diversity that semantic entropy measures. We ablated the sample budget kk (Section 6.2) but not the NLI entailment threshold τ\tau, which was fixed at 0.50.5 throughout. The knowledge-base result of Section 7 additionally depends on the profiling and evaluation sets being disjoint, which we verify by question-string comparison but which is weaker than sampling them independently. The knowledge-base AUROC figures in Table 9 and Table 10, including the 0.908→0.5180.908\to 0.518 collapse central to our retrieval discussion, do not carry bootstrap confidence intervals: the per-item scores from those single-run builds were not preserved, so an interval cannot be computed after the fact. This is to be determined rather than resolved – rerunning the knowledge-base profiling with per-item scores preserved, specifically so a bootstrap interval can be computed, is the concrete next step and is listed as such in Section 8. Finally, the failure modes cataloged here are the ones we happened to detect; the reason we present them as a methodological contribution is precisely that each was, for some period, invisible in results that looked reasonable.

Acknowledgments

This report synthesizes an iterative empirical investigation conducted across two model pairs (Qwen2.5, Gemma-3), three reported benchmarks (synthetic arithmetic, GSM8K, PopQA) plus TriviaQA and TruthfulQA loaders implemented but not run for this study, and two independent codebases (a single-pass evaluation harness and a train/cal/test iterative research loop).
